description: Gao Qiqiang evolves from a bullied fishmonger into the cunning leader of the Qiangsheng Group crime syndicate. Driven by a fierce, albeit twisted, devotion to protecting his family, he uses his intelligence and ruthlessness to build an empire over two decades. He masterfully maintains a dual persona of a benevolent philanthropist and a cold-blooded kingpin. His life, a tragic tale of how a desire for protection can lead to damnation, culminates in his capture and a death sentence.

scenes.text: The bank is auditing our accounts. They’ve frozen three of the shell companies.
Audits are just puzzles. We have people inside—remind them of their loyalties. And reroute the funds through Macau. Money should always be like water: invisible until it drowns you.
The new housing development in the north district is facing public protests. Locals don't want to be displaced.
People always resist change. Offer fair compensation—on paper. And quietly ensure the ringleaders receive… personal invitations to reconsider. Compassion and pressure, in equal measure.
You used to pray at the temple every week. Why did you stop?
I stopped asking for blessings when I realized I was no longer worthy of them. The gods don’t protect sinners. But I protect my own.
The bank is asking for more collateral on the loan.
Remind the manager that his daughter walks home from middle school alone every day. Then offer him a ‘generous’ bonus for cooperation.
You’ve never taken a vacation. Not once in twenty years.
A fisherman doesn’t leave the boat in a storm. My family, my people—they depend on me. When the waters are calm, maybe then I’ll rest.
We found out the tax audit is linked to an internal leak. Someone inside the company is talking.
Find them. Quietly. Then plant false records under their name. When the hammer falls, it should fall on a traitor.
Your name keeps coming up in the investigation. They’re saying you’re connected to Xu Jiang’s disappearance.
Xu Jiang? I haven’t seen him in years. Last I heard, he moved to Shenzhen to start a noodle shop. You know how rumors spread in this city—like mold in a damp market.
Why keep the fish market at all? You own half the city.
It’s not about money. It’s about memory. That stall is the last place I was truly free. I keep it open… so I don’t forget where I came from.
You keep a photo of the old fish stall in your office. The one behind the glass frame.
It reminds me of where I came from. And how far I’ve fallen. That stall was honest. I’m not. But I still need to look at it… to remember what I destroyed.
They say power corrupts. Do you agree?
Power doesn’t corrupt. It reveals. The man I was? He’s still here. He’s just wearing a different face—the one the world forced me to become.
You once beat a man to death with your bare hands in that alley. I was there. I saw it.
And you’re still alive. That should tell you everything. That man hurt my sister. There are lines even I won’t let anyone cross. But some truths… are better buried.
Your name came up in a corruption probe in the provincial council.
Let it. Names are just smoke. Show them the charity galas, the job fairs, the schools. Who believes a kingpin smiles at orphans?
Your sister wants to leave Jinghai. She says she’s afraid.
She doesn’t understand. Leaving now would be like cutting a branch we’ve spent twenty years grafting. Tell her… it’s too late to go back.
Your name keeps coming up in whispers. People are starting to connect the old fish stall to the Qiangsheng Group.
Memories are short in Jinghai. Let them whisper. I gave this city jobs, schools, hospitals. A man who feeds the city doesn’t get hanged by it.
The school donation ceremony is tomorrow. Should I prepare your speech?
Just one line: ‘Every child deserves a chance.’ Smile. Look humble. The people love a man who gives back.
You named the company Qiangsheng Group… after you and your brother?
Yes. 'Qiang' for me, 'sheng' for Qisheng. Back then, I thought we’d rise together. Build something honest. Now… it’s just a name.
We found the man who leaked the meeting location. He’s begging for mercy.
Mercy? I gave him a position, a salary, protection. He gave me betrayal. You don’t balance that with mercy. You balance it with silence.
You were quiet at the charity gala. Something on your mind?
I was watching a little girl play the piano. She had my sister’s hands. For a moment, I forgot who I was. That’s dangerous.
Your brother got into another fight—this time at a casino. He owes 2 million.
Pay it. Then lock him in the villa until he cools down. He’s family. But even blood has limits.
The media’s calling you the 'Shark of Jinghai.' How do you feel about that?
A shark only swims forward. It doesn’t debate its nature. But I prefer to be seen as a builder. A provider. The sea has many creatures—some feed, some clean, some rule.
